column3: Two projectiles launch simultaneously from the same level: A is thrown vertically up at 20 m s⁻¹; B, from a point 30 m horizontally away, has horizontal speed 10 m s⁻¹ and vertical speed 20 m s⁻¹ toward A. Neglect air resistance. When do their horizontal positions first coincide, and are their heights then equal?
column9:
Answer: (B) At 3 s, equal heights.
Given: Horizontal gap 30 m; B's horizontal speed 10 m s⁻¹; vertical initial velocities equal.
Formula/Principle: Relative horizontal position closes at 10t=30; vertical displacements are both 20t−gt²/2.
Step 1: t=3 s; at that instant the vertical coordinates are equal for any common g.
Worked derivation: \[x_B-x_A=30-10t=0\Rightarrow t=3\,\mathrm s;\quad y_A=y_B=20t-	frac12gt^2.\]
Why: Equal vertical initial velocities and equal gravitational acceleration maintain equal height throughout the flight, so only horizontal closure needs solving. At g≈10, both are 15 m above launch level at 3 s.
Why not the others: (A) closes only 20 m; (C) ignores the identical vertical motion; (D) passes horizontal alignment.
Key point: Separate independent horizontal and vertical motions.

column3: A constant horizontal force 12 N moves a cart at instantaneous velocity 3 m s⁻¹ along the force. What is instantaneous mechanical power delivered?
column9:
Answer: (C) 36 W.
Given: Force and velocity are parallel.
Formula/Principle: P=F·v=Fv cosθ.
Step 1: θ=0 and P=12×3=36 W.
Worked derivation: \[P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=(12)(3)\cos0=36\,\mathrm W.\]
Why: Power is work per unit time at the current velocity, so the distance travelled so far is not needed. A perpendicular force would deliver zero instantaneous power even with the same magnitude.
Why not the others: (A) divides force by speed; (B) adds magnitudes; (D) uses a wrong product.
Key point: Use the force component along velocity.

column3: A satellite rotates about a fixed point with negligible external torque. Its moment of inertia changes from I to I/4 while its angular speed initially is ω. What is the final angular speed?
column9:
Answer: (D) 4ω.
Given: External torque is negligible.
Formula/Principle: Angular momentum L=Iω remains constant.
Step 1: Iω=(I/4)ωf.
Worked derivation: \[\omega_f= rac{I}{I/4}\omega=4\omega.\]
Why: Pulling mass closer to the rotation axis decreases inertia, so angular speed rises to conserve momentum. Rotational kinetic energy may change because internal work is done; it need not be constant.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the ratio; (B) halves rather than quarters inertia; (C) misses a factor two.
Key point: Conserve angular momentum, not automatically kinetic energy.

column3: Ideal incompressible water flows from a wide lower pipe at speed 2 m s⁻¹ to a narrow section 1 m higher at speed 4 m s⁻¹. With ρ=1000 kg m⁻³ and g=10 m s⁻², what is p_lower−p_upper?
column9:
Answer: (A) 16 kPa.
Given: Speeds 2,4 m s⁻¹ and elevation difference +1 m.
Formula/Principle: Bernoulli p+½ρv²+ρgh=constant along streamline.
Step 1: Pressure difference=½ρ(4²−2²)+ρg(1)=6000+10000 Pa.
Worked derivation: \[p_l-p_u=	frac12(1000)(16-4)+(1000)(10)(1)=16000\,\mathrm{Pa}=16\,\mathrm{kPa}.\]
Why: Pressure pays for both the kinetic-energy increase and the elevation gain. Using only one of those terms gives an incomplete drop. The higher outlet has both greater gravitational potential per unit volume and greater kinetic energy per unit volume.
Why not the others: (B) omits elevation; (C) omits speed; (D) adds the lower kinetic energy twice.
Key point: Retain both height and speed changes in Bernoulli's equation.

column3: Two different ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure are allowed to mix in an insulated rigid vessel. No chemical reaction occurs. Which statement about entropy of the combined system is correct?
column4: It decreases because diffusion orders molecules
column5: It increases due to additional accessible mixing arrangements
column6: It remains fixed because temperature is unchanged
column7: It changes sign depending only on molar mass
column9:
Answer: (B) It increases.
Why: Removing the partition gives each gas access to more spatial arrangements while total energy is unchanged in the ideal-gas approximation. For distinct gases, the additional mixing microstates raise entropy even when initial temperatures and pressures agree.
Why not the others: (A) reverses accessible-state reasoning; (C) entropy depends on accessible configurations as well as temperature; (D) molar mass alone does not set the sign.
Worked derivation: \[\Delta S_{m mix}=-R(n_A\ln x_A+n_B\ln x_B)>0\quad	ext{for }0<x_A,x_B<1.\]
Key point: Equal temperature does not imply zero entropy of mixing.

column3: A string fixed at both ends has its third harmonic at 120 Hz. Keeping tension and length fixed, what is the frequency of its fifth harmonic?
column9:
Answer: (C) 200 Hz.
Given: f₃=3f₁=120 Hz.
Formula/Principle: Allowed fixed-end frequencies fₙ=n v/(2L).
Step 1: f₁=40 Hz; f₅=5×40=200 Hz.
Worked derivation: \[f_5= rac53 f_3= rac53(120)=200\,\mathrm{Hz}.\]
Why: Changing the harmonic number changes the number of antinodes while wave speed and string length remain unchanged. Node positions shift, but the fundamental spacing remains 40 Hz.
Why not the others: (A) inverses the ratio; (B) uses fourth harmonic; (D) multiplies by five without dividing by three.
Key point: Harmonic frequencies scale with their integer mode number.

column3: Using the two circular orbital states and their radii in the figure, what is the increase in total orbital mechanical energy for the satellite?
column9:
Answer: (D) GMm/(4r).
Given: Initial/final circular radii r and 2r.
Formula/Principle: Circular-orbit total energy E(R)=−GMm/(2R).
Step 1: Ei=−GMm/(2r), Ef=−GMm/(4r).
Worked derivation: \[\Delta E=E_f-E_i=- rac{GMm}{4r}+ rac{GMm}{2r}= rac{GMm}{4r}.\]
Why: The higher orbit is less tightly bound, so its total energy is less negative and must increase. The kinetic energy itself decreases, demonstrating why kinetic energy alone cannot be used as transfer cost.
Why not the others: (A) reverses final minus initial; (B) uses the full initial binding magnitude; (C) gives a negative twice-as-large change.
Key point: Use total circular-orbit energy for each endpoint.

column3: In the charge diagram, at which listed point on the x-axis is the net electric field zero?
column9:
Answer: (A) x=−3a.
Given: Opposite-sign charges at 0 and 3a, magnitudes q and 4q.
Formula/Principle: Fields reinforce between opposite charges. Outside, equate magnitudes.
Step 1: Left of 0 let distance to +q be s; distance to −4q is s+3a. Then s+3a=2s.
Worked derivation: \[s=3a,\qquad x=-s=-3a.\]
Why: Cancellation can occur only outside the interval on the side of the smaller charge. At x=−3a the −4q is twice as far and its fourfold charge is exactly offset by inverse-square distance.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) lie between charges where fields reinforce; (D) is outside on the stronger-charge side where equality is impossible.
Key point: Establish field directions before equating magnitudes.

column3: A capacitor C charged to voltage V is disconnected from its source and then connected in parallel, positive to positive, to an identical uncharged capacitor. What fraction of initial stored electrostatic energy remains in the two capacitors?
column9:
Answer: (B) One half.
Given: Initial charge Q=CV; total final capacitance 2C at fixed net Q.
Formula/Principle: Ui=Q²/(2C); Uf=Q²/[2(2C)].
Step 1: Uf/Ui=1/2.
Worked derivation: \[ rac{U_f}{U_i}= rac{Q^2/(4C)}{Q^2/(2C)}= rac12.\]
Why: The shared final voltage is V/2. Charge is conserved across isolated conductors, while energy decreases as currents dissipate energy in the connecting circuit; it is not conserved as electrostatic storage.
Why not the others: (A) squares voltage without counting doubled capacitance; (C) assumes storage energy conservation; (D) assumes voltage stays fixed by a battery.
Key point: Choose the invariant charge after disconnection.

column3: In a conductor, free-electron density is 1.0×10²⁸ m⁻³ and drift-speed magnitude is 1.0×10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. Taking e=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, what is conventional current-density magnitude?
column9:
Answer: (C) 1.6×10⁵ A m⁻².
Given: n=10²⁸ m⁻³, e=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, vd=10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: |J|=nevd.
Step 1: Powers sum 28−19−4=5.
Worked derivation: \[|J|=(10^{28})(1.6	imes10^{-19})(10^{-4})=1.6	imes10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}.\]
Why: Electron drift direction is opposite conventional current, but the requested magnitude is positive. Multiplying density, charge and speed also produces the correct A/m² dimension.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) lose powers of ten; (D) adds an extra factor ten.
Key point: Use number density, not total electron count.

column3: A circular current loop's radius doubles while its current halves. What happens to magnetic-field magnitude at the centre?
column9:
Answer: (D) One quarter.
Why: The centre field for a circular loop scales as I/R. Halving current supplies a factor 1/2 and doubling radius another 1/2, making 1/4 overall, with the current direction unchanged.
Why not the others: (A) reverses radius dependence; (B) assumes factors cancel; (C) accounts for only one of the two changes.
Worked derivation: \[B= rac{\mu_0 I}{2R},\quad  rac{B'}B= rac{(I/2)/(2R)}{I/R}= rac14.\]
Key point: Compare proportional factors before substituting constants.

column3: A series AC circuit contains R=30 Ω and net inductive reactance X=40 Ω. With rms supply voltage 100 V, what is mean real power?
column9:
Answer: (A) 120 W.
Given: Impedance magnitude √(30²+40²)=50 Ω.
Formula/Principle: Irms=Vrms/Z; P=Irms²R=Vrms Irms cosφ.
Step 1: Irms=100/50=2 A; cosφ=30/50=0.6.
Worked derivation: \[P=I_{m rms}^{2}R=(2)^2(30)=120\,\mathrm W=100(2)(0.6).\]
Why: The reactive voltage component affects current and phase but does not consume average real power in ideal reactance. Using V²/R as though the entire supply were across the resistor would greatly overstate power.
Why not the others: (B) uses apparent power VI; (C) uses a wrong current; (D) squares supply voltage with an incorrect impedance.
Key point: Compute impedance and current before resistive power.

column3: The ray figure places an object 5 cm in front of a concave mirror with focal length 10 cm. Under the Cartesian sign convention, which image distance and nature follow?
column9:
Answer: (B) 10 cm behind, virtual.
Given: u=−5 cm and f=−10 cm.
Formula/Principle: Mirror equation 1/f=1/v+1/u.
Step 1: 1/v=−1/10+1/5=+1/10, hence v=+10 cm.
Worked derivation: \[v=\left( rac1f- rac1uight)^{-1}=\left(- rac1{10}+ rac15ight)^{-1}=+10\,\mathrm{cm}.\]
Why: Object inside the focal length produces diverging reflected rays whose backward extensions meet behind the mirror. Positive v in this convention means a virtual image on the far side.
Why not the others: (A) reverses distance sign; (C) equates object and image distance; (D) places a real image where reflected rays do not meet.
Key point: Interpret sign together with the ray geometry.

column3: Two plane electromagnetic waves propagate in the same medium at equal frequency. If wave B has twice the electric-field amplitude of wave A, what is their mean energy-flux ratio IB/IA?
column9:
Answer: (C) Four.
Why: In the same medium, time-averaged intensity is proportional to the square of electric-field amplitude. Doubling the amplitude makes the energy transported per unit area per unit time four times greater; frequency equality avoids an unrelated comparison.
Why not the others: (A) inverses the trend; (B) assumes linear scaling; (D) cubes the amplitude ratio.
Worked derivation: \[ rac{I_B}{I_A}=\left( rac{E_B}{E_A}ight)^2=2^2=4.\]
Key point: Energy flux follows field amplitude squared.

column3: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks around intermediate mass numbers and is lower for very light nuclei. Which process involving only light nuclei can release energy according to this curve?
column4: Splitting light nuclei into lighter pieces
column6: Fusing beyond the heavy end regardless of product
column7: Fusing light nuclei toward the peak
column9:
Answer: (D) Fusing toward the peak.
Why: Greater binding energy per nucleon means the final nucleons are more tightly bound and the total mass-energy is lower. Fusion of sufficiently light nuclei toward the intermediate peak can therefore release the mass difference as energy.
Why not the others: (A) generally moves away from stronger binding for light nuclei; (B) produces no binding change; (C) asserts release without comparing initial and final binding.
Worked derivation: \[Q=B_{m final}-B_{m initial}>0\quad	ext{when total final binding increases}.\]
Key point: Compare total binding, not simply nuclear mass number.
